items.title: Premier League’s burst of early sendings-off may not last – but red cards are on the rise for a reason
items.summary:
While referees tend to reach for red early in the season before easing off, players are under increasing pressure to keep pace in a frenetic environment

Off! Off! Off! The past three Premier League games have featured a red card, each for a different reason. Brighton’s Costinha was sent off for two bookings at Hull, Leny Yoro collected a red card against Liverpool for denying a goalscoring opportunity (though his suspension was overturned on appeal) and James Tarkowski saw red for serious foul play at Brentford.

This season is shaping up to be an outlier in the VAR era of officiating in English football. The latest red cards took the Premier League total to 22 in 2026-27. The rate of 0.2 per game equates to 76 across the whole season, which would equal the Premier League record set in 2005-06. Refereeing has evolved in the past decade, though. The average across the seven completed campaigns since VAR was introduced is 0.12 per game, with a high of 0.15 in 2023-24.

items.t: Premier League’s burst of early sendings-off may not last – but red cards are on the rise for a reason

items.title: From Test discards to emerging talents: how Australia’s batting contenders shape up | Martin Pegan
items.summary:
One or perhaps more spots are up for grabs ahead of the summer series against New Zealand. We assess the leading batters’ chances of being picked in the XI

Australia’s cricketers would be within their rights to be counting down the days until attention turns to the first Test of the home summer against New Zealand in Perth. As the sandpapergate scandal overshadows a pair of white-ball series against arch-rivals England, batters around the country have been pressing their claims for a place in Australia’s XI when the Chappell-Hadlee Trophy series begins on 9 December.

A vacancy has already opened at the top of the order after selectors took the unusual step to confirm earlier this month that Marnus Labuschagne had been dropped from the squad for the four-Test series. The race to replace Australia’s No 3 – whether slotting straight into Labuschagne’s spot at first drop or as part of a batting order reshuffle – has become packed with Test discards and an emerging talent hoping to earn a debut. The door could open for more than one addition to the XI alongside presumed incumbents Travis Head, Matt Renshaw, Steve Smith, Cameron Green, Josh Inglis and wicketkeeper Alex Carey, with worrying signs Australia’s ageing squad is starting to creak after three defeats in their past five Tests.

Continue reading...

items.title: ‘He’s more elegant’: Bellingham downplays Zidane comparisons after wondergoal
items.summary:
Englishman hailed by teammates and manager Mourinho after coming on to completely change Champions League game against PSV Eindhoven

“It was one of those moments when you’re just: ‘Wow.’” Bernardo Silva had a good view of Jude Bellingham scoring the goal, the golazo, that put Real Madrid into the lead and the Bernabéu on its feet, shock giving way to song, naa, naa, naa, na-na-na-naa, na-na-na-naa ringing round again. “I have no idea what I did,” the Englishman said afterwards. What he did was turn all Le Tissier. Lifting the ball with his left, raising it with his right, twisting and not letting it drop, he sent it arching from the outside of his boot into the far corner, something straight out of the 90s.

“I just kind of hit it,” Bellingham reckoned; not wanting to hit it too hard, it had gone “looping”, “stabbing”, he said. “Normally [my goals are] a lot closer, aren’t they? I was a bit surprised, honestly. Normally from there I’m looking to see who is an option to play it through to, but it popped up nicely. It was nice.” Nice? It was, Silva said, “special”. A “work of art” Marca called it. The presenter on one radio station claimed it was the best goal he had ever seen, and it wasn’t just him; wasn’t just the goal, either.

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘He’s more elegant’: Bellingham downplays Zidane comparisons after wondergoal

items.title: Senegal regaining Afcon title is the right end to embarrassing farrago but issues do not stop here | Osasu Obayiuwana
items.summary:
After African football was dragged into needless disrepute the next step is to tackle two key areas of governance

A journey of 310 days and three legal proceedings to confirm two things we know – that Senegal beat Morocco 1-0 to win the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations and, most importantly, that the decision of a referee remains final and sacrosanct – has produced the longest, most comical and embarrassing Afcon final in the tournament’s 69-year history.

As the Confederation of African Football (Caf) executive committee member Samir Sobha told the Guardian, the decision of the organisation’s appeals board in March to overturn Senegal’s victory and award the title to Morocco, prompting a legal charade ended by the court of arbitration for sport’s verdict on Tuesday, was a “big joke” that brought Caf and the Afcon into needless disrepute.

items.title: Will Hajime Moriyasu get a high-profile job in Europe after his eight years in charge of Japan?
items.summary:
The coach will leave early after the postponement of the Asian Cup and, while there has been clear progress, some had hoped for better results at World Cups

A popular Christmas tradition in Japan is to head to KFC but there is an unexpected item on the menu to chew over this year for the millions who do so – a meaty debate over Hajime Moriyasu’s eight years as national-team head coach. Among the many consequences of the Asian Cup’s postponement from January 2027 to December is the fact his tenure has ended early.

The 58-year-old was supposed to stay on until February to cap that lengthy spell with (hopefully) a deserved trophy, hand over to Go Oiwa and then, perhaps, blaze a trail to Europe. Instead he left this month, after 113 games in charge during which Japan became a global force to be reckoned with, even if there are those who think he underdelivered.

Four umpires discuss how they deal with players, why they avoid social media, how technology is changing cricket and why umpiring beats being a football referee

By Wisden Cricket Monthly

Last summer, sat in a quiet ground at the fag-end of a four-dayer, with a few souls still kicking around and a clutch of cameras streaming what was left of the day live on YouTube, it struck me again what a great, strange sanctuary this place is, out there on the edges of the modern world. The game is trying to move, albeit at its own pace. Later that night, the day’s highlights would be landing on social media, available to all, for the game’s devotees to pore over and pick apart.

More people are watching the County Championship than ever before. Streaming numbers show a growing audience in the UK and a widening uptake across the cricketing globe. The numbers aren’t yet earth-shattering, but how could they be, with such eccentric fare?

items.title: The story of how Pelé and Maradona went from friends to bitter rivals
items.summary:
A new book charts the complicated relationship between the two legends, starting on a sunny afternoon in Rio in 1979

Pelé and Diego Maradona first met in April 1979, not long after the Argentinian led his country’s under-20 side to the finals of the World Youth Cup. Maradona told a journalist friend that his dream was to meet the Brazilian, and after a few weeks of aborted attempts to bring them together – mostly because Diego did not want to travel on a Monday, the one day he had free for his girlfriend Claudia – the meeting finally took place in Rio.

Reporter Guillermo Blanco, who was writing about the meeting for Argentinian sports magazine El Gráfico, got the OK from Pelé’s people and was so intent on making it happen that he checked Maradona onto a flight one Sunday night without telling him. He collared the young man after Argentine Juniors played Huracán and then raced to the airport and put him on a plane with his father, his agent and a photographer.

items.t: The story of how Pelé and Maradona went from friends to bitter rivals

items.title: Gukesh escapes time crisis to draw world chess championship opener with Sindarov
items.summary:

  • Defending champion plays white in Game 2

  • Read our move-by-move report of Game 1

  • Sindarov: ‘I can’t play games just for fun’

Indian chess star Gukesh Dommaraju held off Javokhir Sindarov amid a mounting time crisis on Tuesday, drawing the opening game of their eagerly awaited $2.5m world title match in 38 moves at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in the picturesque Geneva suburb of Cologny.

After spending more than 36 minutes on a single move and much of the afternoon racing against the clock, the defending champion said the time he invested early helped him play faster as a drawish position sharpened and his minutes dwindled opposite the in-form Uzbek challenger. “When I got into the time trouble, I’d already thought about the next few moves,” Gukesh said. “And then the moves after that were pretty easy.”
items.t: Gukesh escapes time crisis to draw world chess championship opener with Sindarov

items.title: Jannik Sinner’s Australian Open appearance in doubt after knee surgery
items.summary:
• Wimbledon champion sidelined since winning title

  • ‘We’ve tried everything to treat injury without surgery’

Jannik Sinner faces further time off the court after undergoing knee surgery. The former world No 1 has been sidelined with pain in his right knee since winning his second consecutive Wimbledon title in July.

Details on Sinner’s condition have been scarce but on Tuesday he announced he has had a minor operation on his iliotibial band in an attempt to solve the problem. While no timeline for recovery has yet been set out, it seems almost certain to rule out a comeback for the Australian Open in January, as had been the intention.

items.title: Teen star Vaibhav Sooryavanshi blitzes through record books with 53-ball 204
items.summary:
• India A batter breaks sixes record with 28 against UAE

  • Captain Tilak Varma: ‘I would say it’s absolute carnage’

The teenage sensation Vaibhav Sooryavanshi hammered 204 off 53 balls for India A on Tuesday to break a host of records, including for the fastest century and double-century in List A cricket.

The 15-year-old Sooryavanshi struck a staggering 28 sixes, the most in a senior men’s innings, as India passed their target of 250 against the United Arab Emirates in just 14.2 overs.

items.title: Cowan-Dickie insists England will not let up after record triumph over All Blacks
items.summary:
• Hooker was involved in 2019 win against New Zealand

  • ‘The way we trained today, I don’t see any complacency’

Luke Cowan-Dickie is adamant England will not let complacency creep in after their record win over the All Blacks, insisting they will not repeat the mistakes of the 2019 World Cup.

Cowan-Dickie is one of three players, with Jamie George and Maro Itoje, who would claim a fourth career win for England against New Zealand on Saturday if Steve Borthwick’s side back up last weekend’s 37-12 victory at Twickenham. The Sale hooker was part of the squad who defeated the All Blacks in the 2019 World Cup semi-final in emphatic fashion and went into the final against South Africa as favourites. Eddie Jones’s side were comfortably outplayed by the Springboks, however, with Cowan-Dickie acknowledging that England failed to hit their emotional peak that day.

items.t: Cowan-Dickie insists England will not let up after record triumph over All Blacks
